REPUBLIC OF TAJIKISTAN

Tajikistan Women’s Economic Empowerment Project (TWEEP)

Grant No.: TF-D1600 (TWEEP, P511398)

Assignment Title: Conducting a Baseline Survey for the TWEEP Project

Reference No. (as per Procurement Plan): TWEEP-CS-CQS-01

The Government of the Republic of Tajikistan has received financing in the amount of US$4.73 million from the World Bank toward the cost of the Tajikistan Women’s Economic Empowerment Project (TWEEP) and intends to apply part of the proceeds for consulting services.

The consulting services (“Services”) include the engagement of a consulting firm to conduct the Baseline Survey for the TWEEP Project. The objective of the assignment is to collect and analyze baseline data to assess the subsequent progress and results of the Project in accordance with its Results Framework indicators. The selected consulting firm will develop and agree on the survey methodology and sampling plan, prepare and program the survey instruments in the CAPI system, conduct pre-testing and field piloting of the questionnaires, organize training of field staff, data collection and quality control, data cleaning and analysis, and prepare a final analytical report on the results of the Baseline Survey.

The assignment will include conducting 1,080 interviews in six target districts of the Project, including 1,000 interviews with women and 80 interviews with existing MSMEs led or managed by women. In addition, the consulting firm will organize and conduct 12 Focus Group Discussions (FGDs), two in each Project district, with approximately 8–10 participants in each group.

The firm will also be responsible for developing a detailed fieldwork plan, translating the survey instruments into the relevant languages, programming the questionnaires in the CAPI system, regularly monitoring fieldwork, conducting back-checks, spot-checks and other data quality assurance activities, preparing cleaned databases in Excel, SPSS and Stata formats, conducting quantitative and qualitative data analysis, and preparing the final report in English and Russian.

The expected duration of the consulting services is 6 (six) months from the date of contract signing.

The Terms of Reference (TOR) for this assignment can be found at the following link:

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gv7XTFcscnOfgOsxwWLJqxjwRv0_QRloLLE8XLiOUAY/edit?usp=sharing

The State Committee on Investments and State Property Management of the Republic of Tajikistan (SCISPM), through its Project Implementation Group (PIG), now invites eligible consulting firms (“Consultants”) to indicate their interest in providing the Services. Interested Consultants should provide information demonstrating that they have the required qualifications and relevant experience to perform the Services.

Shortlisting Criteria

Expressions of Interest will be evaluated based on the following criteria:

(i) At least 5 years of experience in conducting comparable large-scale household surveys in Tajikistan, including at least five surveys involving no fewer than 1,000 respondents each using a Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) system;

(ii) Availability of qualified key personnel, including field interviewers, to conduct the baseline evaluation study;

(iii) Direct experience in collecting research data in Tajikistan among entrepreneurs; knowledge or experience in interviewing women in rural areas will be considered an advantage; and

(iv) Experience in carrying out similar assignments under projects financed by international financial organizations, including the World Bank or other donors.

Key experts will not be evaluated at the shortlisting stage.

The attention of interested Consultants is drawn to Section III, paragraphs 3.14, 3.16 and 3.17 of the World Bank’s Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers, September 2025 (“Procurement Regulations”), setting forth the World Bank’s policy on conflict of interest.

Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD)-Djibouti

Request for Expression of Interest

Project No.: (P178566)

 

 Grant No: IDA-E 0820

 

Assignment Title: Consultancy for compiling baseline information on soil/fertilizer policies, fertilizer usage and soil health best practices in IGAD Region

Contract No.: DJ-IGAD-567394-CS-INDV

The Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) has received financing from International Development Agency (IDA) towards the cost of the Food systems resilience program for Eastern and Southern Africa and intends to apply part of the proceeds of this Grant to payments under this contract: Consultancy for compiling baseline information on soil/fertilizer policies, fertilizer usage and soil health best practices in IGAD Region

  1. Objectives of the Assignment

The main objectives of the assignment are:

  1. To Assess existing policy, institutional, financial and technical opportunities and gaps affecting fertilizer access and sustainable soil management.
  2. To map out the current status of soil health management initiatives, including: Soil fertility management, Soil conservation; Integrated Soil Fertility Management (ISFM), Climate-smart soil management, Regenerative agriculture, Organic nutrient management, Precision agriculture.
  3. Document available soil information systems including, Soil laboratories; Soil testing services
  4. To document best practices, innovations and success stories on sustainable soil and fertilizer management.
  5. Recommend directions for strengthening regional collaboration, policy harmonization and investment.
  1. Scope of the consulting services and specific tasks

The study will focus on the IGAD Region and Member states including Djibouti, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, Uganda.

The specific tasks will include: 

  1. Map out the existing soil and fertilizer policies, fertilizer usage and soil health best practices in IGAD Region
  2. Literature review and data collection from governments, research institutions, development partners and regional organizations
  3. Preparation of Data collection tool and Key informant interviews with relevant stakeholders;
  4. Conduct a Review of existing Regional and national policies including gap analysis and recommendations for harmonization and investment, strategies or guidelines, including cross border agreements between countries. Regional inventory of soil and fertilizer policies, fertilizer use and consumption and recommendation systems, Soil health status profile for each Member State; database of soil laboratories and information systems, regional best practices.
  5. Validation of compiled information with Member States

3. Minimum Consultant’s qualifications and experience requirements

  • The consultant should possess 5 years of experience in Agriculture, Soil Science, Agronomy, Plant Nutrition, Natural Resource Management and communication skills.
  • Clear understanding of Regional Policy processes and experience policy analyses.
  • Clear understanding of Good Agricultural Practices related to soil Health and Fertilizer use efficiency.
  • Experience in Integrated Soil Fertility Management, ISFM Practices.
  • Experience in IGAD Region Agro-ecology and Integrated Sustainable Land and Management
  • Good knowledge of African agricultural policy frameworks, including CAADP, the Africa Fertilizer and Soil Health Action Plan, and sustainable land management initiatives.
  • Good Communication, analytical and Reporting Skills.

4. The Consulting Services Contract is expected to be for a period of Six (6) calendar months from the contract commencement date.

5.The Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) now invites individuals to express their interest in providing the services. Interested individuals must provide information indicating that they are qualified to perform the services (attach curriculum vitae (CV), copies of documentary evidence of Academic qualifications, and Professional Qualifications.

6. An Individual Consultant will be selected in accordance with the Selection of Individual Consultants method set out in the World Bank’s Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers dated November 2020 (Regulations).

7. Interested individuals may obtain further information at the address below from 0900 to 1700 hours East African Time (EAT) from Monday to Friday EAT).

Expression of interest shall be sent by e-mail by 20th of September, 2026 at 1700hours EAT to:procurement@igad.int copy: hassan.salah@igad.int , with subject line ‘‘FSRP- Consultancy for compiling baseline information on soil/fertilizer policies, fertilizer usage and soil health best practices in IGAD Region, CONTRACT NO-.: DJ-IGAD-567394-CS-INDV ’’.

Agency Description

Participating Countries

The Pacific Island Countries (PICs) participating in the regional project comprise Fiji, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu

The Project development Objective is to enable continuous access to correspondent banking services in the participating Pacific Island Countries

August 2024 to September 30 2030

2. Project Background

The Pacific Island Forum Secretariat (PIFS) is expecting to receive financing from the World Bank (WB) Group’s International Development Association (IDA) for a proposed project to enable continuous access to correspondent banking services in Pacific Island Countries (PICs).  The PICs covered by the proposed regional project (Fiji, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu) include diverse island economies facing similar correspondent banking relationship challenges.

PICs range in size and topography – from small island states such as Samoa, with two principal inhabited volcanic islands, to large archipelagos such as the Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI), with 29 atolls spread over 2 million km2 of ocean. Population sizes vary from 11,300 people in Tuvalu to 930,000 people in Fiji.

The economic landscape of PICs is equally diverse, marked by different growth drivers, poverty rates, and growth trajectories. The average GDP growth across PICs decelerated to 3.5 percent in 2023 after a historically high of 7.9 percent in 2022, in a rebound from the COVID-19 crisis. However, medium-term growth prospects have worsened, with output growth expected to be significantly below the pre-pandemic trend of 4.7 percent between 2014 & 2019. Given low growth and limited employment opportunities in the island economies, labor migration to neighboring countries and the resulting remittances are critical drivers of living standards.

The United States, New Zealand, and Australia account for 94 percent of the Pacific diaspora. Trade and tourism are vital for many PICs, providing revenue and employment opportunities. Remittances, equivalent to more than 40 percent of GDP in some PICs, are a buffer against income shocks and an important source of finance for essential household consumption and human capital investment.

Financial systems in PICs are characterized by low levels of financial access and an uneven development of national payment systems. Both domestically owned and multinational commercial banks dominate the financial sector in all PICs.  In several PICs, much of the population lacks access to basic transaction accounts, limiting households and businesses’ ability to send and receive payments, save, invest, and respond to climatic and economic shocks. The financial market infrastructure is underdeveloped, in part due to limited competition and the lack of economies of scale. The level of national payment system development is uneven across PICs, and regional efforts to improve the efficiency of cross-border payments are limited in scale and scope.

PICs are uniquely vulnerable to the withdrawal of the correspondent banking relationships (CBR) that underpin international trade, tourism, remittances, and humanitarian financial flows. Correspondent banking is an arrangement under which one bank (correspondent) holds deposits owned by other banks (respondents) and provides payment and other services to those respondent banks. CBRs are an essential feature of the global payment system – they enable individuals, businesses, and governments to make and receive cross-border payment services related to remittances, e-commerce, trade, and official sector flows. The cross-border transactions enabled in PICs are in various currencies, primarily the US dollar, Euro, and Australian dollar.

The withdrawal of CBRs, a well-documented global phenomenon affecting many emerging markets and developing economies, has adverse consequences and negative externalities for Pacific Islanders, including seasonal laborers, small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and vulnerable populations. Based on publicly available data, the number of active correspondents for Pacific banks has declined significantly since 2011 to levels that put the Pacific financial system overall at risk.

In order to mitigate the issues identified above, the WB will provide funding to the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat (PIFS) to implement the proposed “Pacific Strengthening Correspondent Banking Relationships Project”.  The Pacific Islands Forum was established to bring together the region to address pressing issues and challenges and foster collaboration and cooperation in pursuing shared goals. PIF’s mandate is to strengthen cooperation and integration in the Pacific region through the pooling of regional governance, resources, and the alignment of policies, furthering Forum members' shared goals of economic growth, sustainable development, good governance, and security. Founded in 1971, it comprises 18 members: Australia, Cook Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Nauru, New Caledonia, New Zealand, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Republic of Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu.    The PIFS is a vital platform for Leaders to convene, engage in discussions, and agree on policies that will benefit the people of the region.

The project will have two components: (1) Temporary correspondent banking services and (2) Enabling environment and regulatory harmonization.  The proposed project will be implemented by a Project Management Unit (PMU) within the PIFS with strategic project oversight provided by a Project Steering Committee (PSC) comprised of representatives of participating Pacific Finance Ministers. While the PMU will be responsible for day-to-day project activities, it will need to ensure close collaboration and coordination with participating Ministries of Finance, which will oversee project activities and approve work plans through the PSC.

Comprising of Secretaries of Finance or other officials from the participating PICs finance ministries and the PIFS Director (Programs and Initiative), the PSC will meet on a quarterly basis and be responsible for the approval of key project activities as needed. The PSC will report to Pacific Finance Ministers annually at the Forum Economic Minister Meeting (FEMM) to ensure that strategic guidance and orientation are provided over the project activities. At the technical level, each participating PIC will be required to nominate a competent   government official as a Country Focal Point (CFP) responsible for project coordination at the national level, who will be designated as the point of contact with the PMU and the WB team.

The competent government official in each PIC will be complemented by a country coordinator (CC) based in-country, recruited through the PMU, and responsible for coordinating service delivery at the individual country level.

The PIFS is now seeking qualified and competent national consultants from each member country to be the country coordinator (CC) for the PMU and based in the respective participating Pacific Island countries (PICs).  The required positions are expected to be selected by the PIFS in accordance with the WB’s ‘Procurement Regulations for Investment Project Financing (IPF) Borrowers’ (Procurement Regulations), Seventh edition, September 2025, and as amended over time.

3. Objective of the Position

The main objective of the CC would be to provide on the ground support to the PMU in managing and coordinating the full range of project, country specific activities. The CC will be funded by the project (through the PMU) and report to the PIFS/ PMU Coordinator.  In addition, he/she will work closely with the specific Country Focal Point (CFP), a government official appointed by the MOF of that particular PIC.

 

 

4. Scope of Services

The CC will be required to adopt a flexible approach to coordinate and facilitate the required country specific project activities and report on tangible outcomes in terms of project implementation progress. The CC will be required to work in a pro-active manner, and to help ensure effective implementation of activities and delivery of outputs in a timely manner.

  1. Liaising with PICs Ministry of Finance’s CFP and Central Bank on country specific project related activities, including follow up on the Project Steering Committee (PSC) meetings and preparing meeting minutes as required;

  9. Prepare the required documentation for the payment of outputs prepared by the selected consultants, obtain CFP approval and submit documents to the PMU for payment;
  10. Work closely with the CFP in preparing annual reports on country specific activities to be submitted to the MOF and PIFS; and
  11. Any other activities as requested by the CFP or the PMU Project Coordinator.

 

5. Reporting Obligations

The CC will attend scheduled virtual meetings with the PMU and provide weekly reports on work done.

6. Institutional Arrangements

This is a part-time work assignment, with the Consultant expected to be based in in their home country. The Consultant will be supported by the PIFS PMU based in Suva, Fiji but will work closely with and report to the country focal person in the first instance. The CC is expected to show flexibility in working arrangements as time inputs will fluctuate based on country requirements. The work will be part-time, averaging approximately 12 days per month (with a total of 144 days in and year and a maximum of 20 days per month) for the next six years. A contract will initially be signed for two years with a performance-based extension every two years thereafter. Performance evaluation shall be the basis for the extension or termination of the services. Facilities such as office space, intercom telephone facilities, personal computers, printing facilities, Internet access and stationery shall be the responsibility of the Country Coordinator.

 

7. Performance Indicators

The following performance indicators shall be used for performance assessment:

  1. Positive progress and good performance of the entrusted project activities, as per the TOR;
  2. Ensuring that WB processes and procedures are complied with in all activities and in accordance with the POM;

To promote the IBRD Guangdong Agricultural Product Quality Safety Improvement (Demonstration) Project and showcase its implementation outcomes, the Guangdong Center for Agricultural Product Quality and Safety (Guangdong Green Food Development Center) intends to engage a Project Publicity Consulting Advisor to provide professional publicity services for the project

 

I.Project Background

Agricultural product quality and safety are critical issues of national importance that directly affect people's livelihoods. In recent years, national authorities have successively introduced policy documents such as the Regulations for the Implementation of the Food Safety Law of the People's Republic of China and the 14th Five-Year Plan for National Agricultural Green Development, explicitly proposing the establishment of a comprehensive quality and safety management system spanning the entire supply chain 'from farm to table'.

As part of the China Food Safety Project, Guangdong Province is responsible for the implementation of the World Bank-financed Guangdong Agricultural Product Quality Safety Improvement (Demonstration) Project. The project comprises four sub-components: Food Safety Supervision Process, Institution Building and Regulatory Performance, Whole Value Chain Food Safety Control, and Project Implementation Support.

II.Objectives of the Consulting Services

By engaging a Consulting Advisor, this project aims to carry out comprehensive publicity activities for the World Bank-financed Guangdong Agricultural Product Quality Safety Improvement (Demonstration) Project, showcase its implementation outcomes, and enhance the project's visibility and public awareness.

III.Scope of Services

The Consulting Advisor shall provide end-to-end services for this project. The main scope of services includes:

(I) Formulate the Publicity Plan

Develop a comprehensive publicity plan for the World Bank-financed Guangdong Agricultural Product Quality Safety Improvement (Demonstration) Project.

(II) Convergent Media Publicity

1.Provincial-level Media Coverage: Conduct regular publicity on provincial-level media platforms covering specific project activities, events, and outcomes. A minimum of ten (10) news reports shall be published.

2.New Media Campaigns: Launch a series of promotional campaigns on new media platforms. Produce and publish a minimum of fifty (50) short videos on platforms such as Douyin and WeChat Channels (Shipinhao). Performance KPIs: Each published video must achieve a minimum of two thousand (2,000) views and five hundred (500) likes.

3.Promotional Videos: Shoot, produce, and edit high-definition (HD) promotional videos for the project to introduce its activities and showcase its outcomes. A minimum of five (5) videos shall be produced, with each video being no less than two (2) minutes in duration.

4.Graphic and Text Promotional Articles: Write a minimum of twenty (20) graphic and text articles related to project activities. At least five (5) of these articles must focus on food safety risk communication. The articles shall be reposted on a minimum of three (3) official social media accounts (WeChat Official Accounts), and each published article must achieve a minimum of one thousand (1,000) views.

(III) Live-streaming Promotion: Conduct live-streaming coverage of project trainings and events (including both photo live-streaming and video live-streaming). Video Live-streaming: A minimum of three (3) sessions shall be conducted, with each lasting no less than one (1) hour. At least one (1) of these sessions must be dedicated to an event focusing on food safety risk communication. Photo Live-streaming: A minimum of two (2) sessions shall be conducted, providing no less than one hundred (100) high-definition (HD) photos per session.

Posters: A minimum of thirty (30) promotional posters shall be designed. Brochures: Brochures may be revised based on existing project brochures, newly designed, or printed according to specific requirements.

(V) Conceptual Promotion: Conduct conceptual promotion at designated venues of the Guangdong Agricultural Product Quality and Safety Center (Guangdong Green Food Development Center). Regularly update the content of visual and text display boards at these venues.

(VI) Event Photography and Videography: Provide photography, videography, and photo collection and processing services for at least five (5) important events, including visits and supervision missions by World Bank experts, as well as project field research.

notice_text:
Request for Expressions of Interest

 

Country: The Republic of the Gambia

Project Title: The Gambia Resilience, Inclusion, Skills and Equity Project RISE

Grant Number: P1729233

Assignment Title: Consultancy to develop the National Nutrition Regulation and Guideline for NaNA

Procurement Method: Individual Consultant Selection (INDV)

Reference No.: GM-CPCU - MOFEA-556550-CS-INDV

 

Background:

The Gambia is a small country with a total area of about 10,690 square kilometers.  It is surrounded on all sides by the Republic of Senegal, except in the West by the Atlantic Ocean. The population is estimated 2.42 million with a high population growth rate of 3.1 percent per year (Census, 2024). The 2017 Human Development Index shows the country rank at 174 out of 189 countries. Efforts to fight poverty have also proven ineffective with poverty levels remaining unchanged in the past decade (the percentage of households living below the poverty line of 1.25 $/day is 48.65 per cent in 2015 (HIS 2015/2016). The average GDP growth of 3 per cent per annum has barely kept up with population growth of 3.1 per cent. Data from the 2019/20 Demographic Health Survey (DHS) showed encouraging results for U5MR having dropped to 34 per 1,000 down from  54 per 1,000 live births in 2013, Maternal Mortality Ratio estimated 189/100,000 down from at 433/100000 live births in 2013.

Micronutrient deficiencies are widespread and continue to pose serious public health risks. Anaemia affects 44.8% of children, and only 10.8% of households consume adequately iodized salt even though 77% do consume iodized salt. Vitamin A deficiency affects 18.3% of children under five (MICS 2018). These figures highlight the urgency of interventions such as supplementation, iodization, fortification, and biofortification, supported by regulatory frameworks like the Food Fortification Regulation (2020). Despite these efforts, gaps in coverage and compliance persist, particularly in rural and underserved communities. Strengthening supply chains, enforcement mechanisms, and public awareness campaigns will be essential to improving micronutrient outcomes.

Infant and young child feeding practices show mixed progress. While 98% of children are breastfed, only 36% of mothers initiate breastfeeding within one hour of birth and 53.6% of children are exclusively breastfed. Complementary feeding remains inadequate, with just 15% of children receiving a minimum acceptable diet. The prevalence of malnutrition has improved with the DHS 2019/20 estimating stunting at 17.5% from 25% in 2013, wasting 5.1% from 12% and underweight 11.6% from 16%. These indicators reflect broader food and nutrition security challenges. The country produces only 50% of its food needs and over half the population (60.2%) do not have enough to meet their food expenditure, according to the Integrated Household Survey (IHS 2022). Climate change, low agricultural productivity, and population growth exacerbate these conditions, prompting national strategies focused on climate-smart agriculture, diversified and increased local food promotion and integration of nutrition into broader development efforts.

Non-communicable Diseases (NCDs) are on the rise, driven by poor diets, sedentary lifestyles, and urbanization. Hypertension affects 47% of adults, and obesity is significantly higher among women (20.2%) compared to men (3.9%) (WHO STEPS Survey 2019). Only 6.6% of the population meets WHO physical activity guidelines, reflecting lifestyle shifts associated with urbanization, poor dietary habits and sedentary lifestyles. The Fill the Nutrient Gap analysis 2025 shows that only 29% can afford a healthy diet. National responses focus on prevention by adopting appropriate dietary guidelines and lifestyles through social and behaviour change communication, and multisectoral collaboration. However, implementation remains fragmented, and greater investment in community-based prevention and promotion of healthy behaviours is needed.

As a cross cutting issue, the improvement and implementation of nutrition interventions and programme requires a strong coordination mechanism to avoid duplication and gaps. The National Nutrition Agency (NaNA) was established in 2000 as a semi-autonomous government institution strategically placed under the Office of The Vice President through an Agency Board with the legal mandate to coordinate nutrition and nutrition-related activities and advocate for the mainstreaming of nutrition into the macroeconomic and sectoral policy frameworks, implement nutrition activities, monitor nutrition interventions and programmes, mobilize and manage resources in The Gambia.

The Agency became a legal entity in 2005 through an Act of the National Assembly (Food Act 2005) which is now repealed and replaced by the Nutrition Act 2024. This ensures effective coordination of nutrition interventions across sectors. The Agency serves as the Secretariat to the National Nutrition Council (an inter-Ministerial body chaired by the Vice President), the country Scaling Up of Nutrition (SUN) Movement and the National Alliance for Food Fortification (NAFF).

The Agency was charged with the overall coordination and implementation of the policy with the following core mandates:

  1. Coordination of policy implementation
  2. Implementation of nutrition activities
  3. Secretariat of the National Nutrition Council
  4. Nutrition policy analysis, research and indicative planning
  5. Monitoring of nutrition interventions and programmes
  6. Mobilisation, management and coordination of resources

Following the enactment of the Nutrition Act 2024, there is need to develop a regulation that is critical for establishing and  formalising the multisectoral governance structures that ensure food and nutrition security and better help to understand and implement the Nutrition Act 2024. The regulation will also translate political commitment into actionable, accountable and sustainable interventions. To work on the development of a Nutrition Regulation, The Gambia, Resilience, Inclusion, Skills and Equity (RISE) Project  has sought the expertise of a Legal Expert for the task.

Objective of The Assignment:

The objective of exercise is to review and develop comprehensive nutrition regulation.

Scope of Work and Key Responsibilities:

The scope of the work will cover the following:

  1. Inception meeting to identify areas of focus for the development of the regulation
  2. Map out which provisions of the Nutrition Act 2024 require secondary legislation particularly focusing on:
    1. Establishment of the Nutrition Fund (modalities, management tea composition and areas of usage)
    2. Reference intake of vitamins and minerals in food sources
    3. Prescription of fortification mix
    4. Establishment of fortification coordination platform (NAFF)
  3. Draft a Nutrition Regulation
  4. Conduct consultative meetings to seek the views of the stakeholders on the new draft Nutrition Regulation
  5. Incorporate views and comments in the draft Regulation
  6. Conduct a national validation of the draft regulation
  7. Facilitate review by the Ministry of Justice
  8. Finalize the Regulation and submit for approval by the Minister responsible for Nutrition

The Draftsman will require close collaboration with the NaNA for continued guidance.

4.  Individual Consultant Qualifications and Experience

Given the high level of technical rigor required to carry out the exercise, which is a succinct and analytically sound comprehensive Nutrition Regulation, dedicated human resource capacity is required in terms of time and technical expertise in conducting such a task. National Expert will objectively review the implementation and coordination mechanisms established by the Nutrition Act 2024 and any other relevant mechanisms. Hence an appropriate experienced expert, who is familiar with the development context in The Gambia and having good working experience of drafting regulations will be preferred. The Expert should possess the following qualification and experience:

  • MSc in Law or equivalent
  • At least 5 years’ experience in legal drafting
  • Familiarity with Gambian law and with food, nutrition, or public health legislation
  • Excellent spoken and written English
  • Knowledgeable in computer

  2. Agenda Barrial: La Agenda Barrial es un instrumento técnico-social estratégico de planificación territorial a escala barrial, elaborado de manera participativa con la población, el Gobierno Autónomo Descentralizado, el ahora Ministerio de Infraestructura y Tecnología (MIT) y otros actores locales.

 

Este instrumento define la hoja de ruta para el desarrollo integral del barrio en el corto, mediano y largo plazo, mediante la identificación y priorización de las necesidades del territorio, e incorpora mecanismos de gobernanza local a través de procesos metodológicos adaptados a contextos de vulnerabilidad climática, riesgos naturales y exclusión social.

 

Asimismo, la Agenda Barrial permite la elaboración de diagnósticos urbano- arquitectónico y social, la identificación de riesgos, oportunidades y necesidades, y la priorización participativa de soluciones de hábitat que orientan una hoja de ruta técnica, para la inversión pública, constituyéndose en un insumo para la ejecución posterior de estudios, diseños y obras físicas que determinará un portafolio de proyectos conforme el Hito de Implementación – Paso 8, Elaboración de la Agenda Barrial del Manual Operativo del Proyecto (MOP).

 

  • Portafolio de proyectos: es un listado de proyectos dentro del polígono barrial específico y su entorno inmediato que han sido identificados, analizados y priorizados participativamente en el desarrollo de la Agenda Barrial. Es una herramienta que contiene fichas técnicas de cada proyecto en las cuales indica información pertinente como ubicación, presupuesto estimado, justificación, importancia, viabilidad y el impacto que genera, así como, el diseño del proyecto a nivel de idea, incluyendo el contenido mínimo establecido en la ficha técnica adjunta (Anexo 10).

 

  1. Obra Priorizada: Obra definida por el barrio en un proceso participativo, es una obra de mayor escala, que materializa la visión definida por la comunidad e identificada en el proceso de la Agenda Barrial, busca cumplir todos los objetivos del Programa de Mejoramiento Integral de Barrios (MIB).

 

El alcance, la metodología e hitos del presente proceso se encuentran determinados en el término de referencia y sus anexos.

 

Los términos de referencia detallados para la presente consultoría podrán consultarse en el siguiente enlace: https://www.mit.gob.ec/postulaciones/

El MIT, invita a las firmas consultoras elegibles (“Consultores”) a manifestar sus expresiones de interés en la prestación de los Servicios. Los Consultores interesados deberán proporcionar información que demuestre que tienen las calificaciones requeridas y la experiencia relevante para realizar los Servicios.

 

 

La presente contratación está dirigida a firmas consultoras o asociaciones de firmas legalmente constituidas, con experiencia demostrable en estudios urbanos, diseño urbano–arquitectónico, gestión y participación social y formulación de instrumentos de planificación participativa a escala barrial o urbana.

La firma consultora deberá:

  1. Estar legalmente constituida y habilitada para prestar servicios de consultoría en el país, de conformidad con la normativa vigente.

  3. Acreditar experiencia específica en al menos uno de los siguientes ámbitos:
  • Proyectos de mejoramiento integral de barrios u operaciones similares.
  • Formulación participativa de agendas barriales, planes o programas a escala barrial o urbana.
  • Estudios y diseños definitivos de espacio público, equipamientos comunitarios o intervenciones urbanas en contextos similares al barrio.
  1. Preferentemente, acreditar experiencia previa en proyectos financiados por organismos multilaterales (Banco Mundial u otros), o en proyectos con requerimientos de salvaguardas socioambientales y enfoques transversales similares.

Tipo

Descripción

Monito mínimo por proyecto

Experiencia general. La firma consultora deberá acreditar un mínimo de tres (3) contratos en: ejecución de proyectos financiados por entidades públicas, gobiernos locales, cooperación internacional o multilaterales (BID, Banco Mundial, GIZ, PNUD, instituciones públicas, etc.); programas de urbanismo social o mejoramiento de barrios; Planes de Desarrollo y Ordenamiento Territorial (PDOT) o Planes de Uso y Gestión de Suelos (PUGS).

 

 

El monto acumulado de los contratos acreditados deberá ser superior a USD 100.000

de diseño participativo; proyectos de mejoramiento integral de barrios con componentes sociales y urbanos; proyectos urbanos temporales o planificados con las comunidades; planes de ordenamiento barrial o esquemas urbanos comunitarios; modelos de gestión.

Juan León Mera N26-220 y Av. Orellana, piso 14, en el horario de 08h30 a.m. a 16h00 p.m.

No serán aceptables documentos de respaldo emitidos por el propio consultor o firma consultora.

Este instrumento define la hoja de ruta para el desarrollo integral del barrio en el corto, mediano y largo plazo, mediante la identificación y priorización de las necesidades del territorio, e incorpora mecanismos de gobernanza local a través de procesos metodológicos adaptados a contextos de vulnerabilidad climática, riesgos naturales y exclusión social.

 

Asimismo, la Agenda Barrial permite la elaboración de diagnósticos urbano- arquitectónico y social, la identificación de riesgos, oportunidades y necesidades, y la priorización participativa de soluciones de hábitat que orientan una hoja de ruta técnica, para la inversión pública, constituyéndose en un insumo para la ejecución posterior de estudios, diseños y obras físicas que determinará un portafolio de proyectos conforme el Hito de Implementación – Paso 8, Elaboración de la Agenda Barrial del Manual Operativo del Proyecto (MOP).

  • Portafolio de proyectos: es un listado de proyectos dentro del polígono barrial específico y su entorno inmediato que han sido identificados, analizados y priorizados participativamente en el desarrollo de la Agenda Barrial. Es una herramienta que contiene fichas técnicas de cada proyecto en las cuales indica información pertinente como ubicación, presupuesto estimado, justificación, importancia, viabilidad y el impacto que genera, así como, el diseño del proyecto a nivel de idea, incluyendo el contenido mínimo establecido en la ficha técnica adjunta (Anexo 10).
  1. Obra Priorizada: Obra definida por el barrio en un proceso participativo, es una obra de mayor escala, que materializa la visión definida por la comunidad e identificada en el proceso de la Agenda Barrial, busca cumplir todos los objetivos del Programa de Mejoramiento Integral de Barrios (MIB).

Agency Description

The Pacific Islands Forum was established to bring together the region to address pressing issues and challenges, and foster collaboration and cooperation in the pursuit of shared goals. PIF’s mandate is to strengthen cooperation and integration in the Pacific region through the pooling of regional governance, resources and the alignment of policies, furthering Forum members shared goals of economic growth, sustainable development, good governance and security. Founded in 1971, it comprises 18 members: Australia, Cook Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Nauru, New Caledonia, New Zealand, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Republic of Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu.  The PIFS is a vital platform for Leaders to convene, engage in discussions and agree on policies that will benefit the people of the region.

The Pacific Islands Forum was established to bring together the region to address shared issues and support cooperation. PIF works through regional governance, shared resources and policy alignment to support economic growth, sustainable development, good governance and security. Founded in 1971, it comprises eighteen members: Australia, Cook Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Nauru, New Caledonia, New Zealand, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Republic of Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu.

Participating Countries

The Pacific Island Countries participating in the regional project comprise Fiji, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu. This assignment provides country-specific support to the Republic of the Marshall Islands under the regional project.

Overall Project Objective

The Project Development Objective is to enable continuous access to correspondent banking services in the participating Pacific Island Countries.

Project Length

August 2024 to September 30, 2030

Project Background

The Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat (PIFS) has received financing from the World Bank Group's International Development Association (IDA) for the Pacific Strengthening Correspondent Banking Relationships Project. The project supports participating Pacific Island Countries (PICs) to maintain continuous access to correspondent banking services, and to address underlying payment, regulatory and financial integrity constraints that contribute to de-risking in the region.

PICs are exposed to the withdrawal of correspondent banking relationships (CBRs) that underpin international trade, tourism, remittances, development finance, disaster relief, and humanitarian financial flows. The project provides a short-term CBR safety net while supporting the enabling environment and regional harmonization needed for a medium-term sustainable solution.

Component 2 of the project, Enabling Environment and Regulatory Harmonization, includes support for Payment System Oversight and Regulation. The relevant activity areas include payment systems regulatory harmonization, oversight of national payment systems, and collection of remittance and gender-disaggregated data on usage of financial services. Component 2 also supports payment systems strengthening, CBR Roadmap implementation, the CBR Resilience Index, and the feasibility work for the Pacific Payment Mechanism (PPM), which aims to aggregate payment flows and improve economies of scale.

The Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI) is in the early phase of operationalizing the MAMI. In June 2026, the Governor of MAMI requested support for an advisor to assist with implementation of the Authority's operationalization strategy, including review and tailoring of recommendations from the IMF Monetary and Capital Markets Department technical assistance report, Operationalizing A New Monetary Authority. The request also highlighted the need to establish the national payment system in alignment with the World Bank CBR Strengthening Project's payment system harmonization roadmap.

The IMF report identifies several payment-related priorities for MAMI. These include the development of a National Payments Strategy (NPS), the establishment of payment operations and payment oversight functions, the creation of a stakeholder consultation mechanism and National Payment Council, the preparation of payment operations and oversight procedures, and the design of an Integrated Payment and Clearing System (IPCS) that can combine ACH, RTGS and instant payment functionality in a phased manner. The report also notes that RMI currently has no centralized payment system, that payment services are dominated by checks, that there is no e-money provider, and that electronic payments remain limited outside selected card and POS use cases.

This assignment is designed as payment systems technical assistance under the CBR Project’s Technical Assistance component. It is framed around the project's Payment System Oversight and Regulation activities and is expected to support MAMI in converting payment-related IMF recommendations into a practical work plan, institutional arrangements, operating procedures, oversight tools, stakeholder coordination mechanisms, and capacity building outputs.

Objective of the Position

The main objective of the Payments System Advisor to MAMI is to provide technical advisory support to MAMI for the establishment of a safe, efficient, inclusive and scalable national payments system and payment system oversight function, aligned with the CBR Project, the CBR Roadmap, regional payment system harmonization work, and the emerging design of the PPM.

The Advisor will review the payment-related findings and recommendations in the IMF MCM report and assist MAMI to translate the relevant payment system recommendations into a practical implementation approach for RMI. This will include helping MAMI distinguish payment system actions from broader central banking, governance, accounting, audit, reserve management, HR, communications and corporate services matters, and sequencing the payment system actions in line with MAMI’s institutional capacity, staffing plans and expected operational priorities.

In doing so, the Advisor will consider the small scale of the RMI financial sector, the dominance of checks, limited electronic payment usage, geographic dispersion, government payment needs, remittance costs, digital financial-service developments, and MAMI’s current staffing and institutional capacity.

Scope of Services

The selected Payments System Advisor will provide country-level, time-based technical implementation support for RMI on payment system matters. The work will be coordinated with the PIFS PMU, the PIFS Payment Systems Specialist, the World Bank payments team, IMF MCM and other technical assistance providers as relevant. The Advisor will carry out the following tasks, with timing and level of effort agreed through the 12-month implementation work plan and periodic work planning discussions:

i. Inception, work planning and IMF recommendation mapping

  • Review the IMF MCM report, MAMI Act and related institutional materials, the CBR Project Operations Manual, the CBR Roadmap, available PPM materials, and other relevant documents provided by MAMI, PIFS or the World Bank.
  • Prepare an inception report that identifies the payment-related recommendations requiring action by MAMI and separates them from broader central banking, governance, accounting, audit, reserve management, HR, communications, and corporate services matters.
  • Develop a 12-month implementation roadmap for the establishment of MAMI’s national payments function, with milestones, dependencies, counterpart responsibilities, expected outputs, sequencing assumptions, and coordination points with the World Bank, IMF and PIFS. The roadmap should be aligned with MAMI’s expected recruitment of the Banking Operations Department Executive Manager and Payment Systems Operations Manager, anticipated around December 2026 to January 2027, so that the Advisor’s support helps prepare for, onboard, and transition responsibilities to these key MAMI counterparts.
  • Prepare and periodically update the Advisor’s own assignment work plan, aligned with the 12-month MAMI implementation roadmap, counterpart availability, agreed priorities, in-country inputs, and monthly or quarterly work planning discussions with MAMI, PIFS and the World Bank.
  • Tailor payment system recommendations to the RMI context, including market size, transaction volumes, institutional capacity, staffing constraints, remittance corridors, public sector payment needs, and affordability for banks and end users.

ii. Establishment of MAMI's national payments function

  • Advise MAMI on the operational setup, sequencing, staffing profile and accountabilities for its national payments function, including the Payment Operations Division (POD) and Payment Oversight and Policy Division (OVD) recommended by the IMF report.
  • Provide advice on the separation of payment system operations and payment system oversight responsibilities within MAMI’s payments mandate, including reporting lines, decision processes, internal coordination arrangements, and safeguards to manage potential conflicts between operational and oversight functions.
  • Prepare a short skills and capacity building plan for MAMI staff involved in payment operations, payment oversight, payment      collection, and stakeholder engagement.
  • Assist MAMI to define working procedures and decision flows for its payment system operational and oversight functions, including issue escalation, internal reporting, consultation with supervised or participating institutions, coordination with IT, risk, legal and supervision functions, and referral of matters requiring specialist technical or legal input.

 

iii. National Payments Strategy

  • Support MAMI to develop a National Payments Strategy that sets out a phased modernization agenda for RMI’s national payment system, aligned with the National Financial Inclusion Strategy and coordinated with related work under the CBR Project, regional payment system harmonization agenda, and emerging PPM design.
  • Prepare or support a baseline diagnostic covering domestic and cross-border payment flows, CBRs, government payments, remittances, check usage, card and POS usage, payment access, digital infrastructure, consumer needs, and data gaps.
  • Identify practical measures to increase use of electronic payments, reduce reliance on checks and cash where appropriate, improve government payment flows, support remittance cost reduction, and expand access to payment services for businesses, households and the public sector.
  • Support stakeholder consultations on the NPS, including preparation of consultation materials, meeting notes, issue logs and revisions to the strategy based on feedback received.

iv. Payment infrastructure and IPCS implementation support

  • Advise MAMI on a fit-for-purpose and phased approach to payment infrastructure modernization, including the IMF recommendation for an Integrated Payment and Clearing System combining ACH, RTGS and instant payment functionality.
  • Advise MAMI on the preparation, review and sequencing of high-level business requirements and implementation planning for any future IPCS, including initial electronic clearing for wire transfers and checks, check truncation, settlement arrangements, participant onboarding, service levels, operating schedules and support arrangements. The Advisor will help MAMI frame the requirements and coordinate specialist inputs but will not be responsible for preparing detailed technical specifications or system design documents unless separately agreed with PIFS, MAMI and the World Bank.
  • Assess the sequencing of ACH, RTGS and instant payment functionality based on RMI transaction volumes, costs, operational readiness, risk profile and user needs.
  • Advise MAMI on the issues that should be considered when planning future payment infrastructure, including payment messaging, straight-through processing, ISO 20022 readiness, data security, operational resilience, business continuity, disaster recovery, liquidity risk, settlement risk and participant default arrangements. Where detailed technical design is required, the Advisor will help MAMI identify the issues, review options, and coordinate inputs from specialist payment infrastructure, IT, cybersecurity or World Bank experts.
  • Provide payment system technical inputs to procurement documents, concept notes or options papers for the IPCS, as requested by MAMI and the PMU, subject to World Bank procurement rules and conflict-of-interest restrictions.

v. Payment system oversight, data and risk-based supervision

  • Support MAMI to define a payment system oversight framework covering objectives, scope, standards, tools, reporting, escalation, corrective actions and coordination with other MAMI functions.
  • Advise MAMI on the scope, structure and phased development of oversight procedures for risk-based monitoring of payment systems and payment service providers, including e-money and non-bank PSPs where relevant. The Advisor may prepare outlines, review drafts and support capacity building, but detailed supervisory manuals, examination procedures or legal instruments should be developed with appropriate specialist and legal input as required.
  • Advise MAMI on the payment data and indicators that should be collected for oversight and policy purposes, including payment volumes and values, failed transactions, settlement incidents, fraud, customer complaints, operational incidents, participation, concentration, liquidity risk, credit risk and operational risk. The Advisor may support the development or review of reporting templates in coordination with MAMI, PIFS and the World Bank, but the final templates should be agreed by MAMI and aligned with wider project data requirements.
  • Provide technical inputs to and reviews of payment-related regulations, rules, circulars or supervisory guidance as requested, including on electronic payments, PSPs, system participation and operational risk. This role does not include drafting primary payment system legislation or formal legal opinions.
  • Align oversight tools with relevant international standards and guidance, including the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures, ISO 20022, risk-based supervision practices, consumer protection principles and cyber-resilience expectations applicable to payment systems.
  • Review USDM1-related payment system implications, considering existing RMI AML laws and regulations and MAMI’s current regulatory treatment of USDM1, and advise on whether any payment system oversight, interoperability, reporting, operational risk, consumer safeguard or AML/CFT coordination measures should be reflected in MAMI’s national payment system framework. The Advisor will not provide advice on the sovereign debt, securities law, issuance, redemption, collateral, reserve management or investment aspects of USDM1 except where these issues directly affect payment system oversight or integration.

vi. Coordination, consultation and National Payment Council support

  • Assist MAMI to establish a consultation mechanism with banks, government agencies, SOEs, card schemes, telecom operators, payment service providers, major users and other stakeholders involved in payments modernization.
  • Prepare draft Terms of Reference, membership options, work program and first-year agenda for a National Payment Council or equivalent advisory body.
  • Support MAMI in coordinating with the Ministry of Finance on payment-related services, including government payment flows, account information, reporting expectations, service levels, and inputs to any payment-related SLA or MOU arrangements.
  • Prepare stakeholder maps, consultation papers, meeting agendas, minutes and action trackers to support implementation of the national payments work plan.

vii. Alignment with the CBR Project and regional work

  • Coordinate closely with the PIFS PMU, PIFS Payment Systems Specialist and World Bank payments team to align RMI support with the CBR Project's Component 2 work program.
  • Support RMI inputs into CBR data collection, the CBR Resilience Index and the PPM feasibility and design process, including payment flow data, remittance information, CBR information and stakeholder feedback.
  • Assist MAMI to collect and improve relevant remittance and gender-disaggregated data on the usage of financial services, where feasible and agreed with the PMU and World Bank.
  • Identify areas where RMI can participate in regional harmonization work, including PSP licensing, QR code standards, open banking/open finance, cross-border interoperability and common principles for cross-border data sharing.
  • Coordinate with IMF MCM and other technical assistance providers, through MAMI, PIFS and the World Bank as appropriate, to reduce duplication, sequence inputs, and keep the assignment focused on payment system matters within the agreed CBR Project scope. Where feasible, the Advisor may support periodic coordination discussions, including around the Annual Meetings or Spring Meetings, if requested by MAMI, PIFS or the World Bank.

viii. Capacity building and knowledge transfer

  • Identify MAMI staff training needs, develop a multi-year training plan, and identify opportunities for training and knowledge transfer aligned with MAMI’s payment system mandate, staffing plan and future development priorities.
  • Prepare training materials, practical templates and work aids that MAMI staff can continue to use after the assignment.
  • Identify peer learning opportunities with regional central banks or payment system operators, including short technical exchanges or virtual clinics where appropriate.
  • Provide mentoring to assigned MAMI counterparts and support handover of tools, procedures and work plans before the end of the assignment.

Scope Exclusions

The assignment is limited to payment systems technical assistance and payment-related operationalization of MAMI. The Advisor will not draft the Payment Systems Act, amendments to the Monetary Authority Act, primary legislation, or formal legal opinions.

The Advisor will not provide general central bank advisory services on reserve management, fiscal agency, accounting, audit, human resources, communications, procurement, general governance, or corporate services except where those topics directly affect payment system operations, payment oversight, payment infrastructure or payment-related stakeholder coordination.

Time-Based Reporting Obligations and Expected Outputs

This assignment will be contracted on a time-based basis. Payments will be linked to approved timesheets, agreed input days, and eligible reimbursable expenses, not to a fixed-price deliverables schedule. The outputs listed below are expected working products and reporting instruments for managing the assignment, tracking progress, supporting quality review, and documenting knowledge transfer.

The Advisor will prepare and update working products in line with the agreed work plan and counterpart needs. These may include the inception note and 12-month payments work plan, IMF recommendation mapping, National Payments Strategy materials, payment function setup notes, National Payment Council materials, payment operations and oversight procedures, data templates, IPCS options and requirements notes, training materials, mission notes and handover materials.

Because the role is advisory and embedded with MAMI for a substantial part of the assignment, outputs may be revised or reprioritized during implementation with agreement from MAMI, PIFS and the World Bank. The Advisor will document changes through monthly activity notes, quarterly progress notes and the action tracker.

Reporting Obligations

The Payments System Advisor will work closely with MAMI on a day-to-day technical basis and will report administratively to the Project Coordinator within the PIFS PMU. Technical priorities, work planning, and expected outputs will be agreed with MAMI, PIFS and the World Bank payments team. The Advisor will also coordinate with the PIFS Payment Systems Specialist and the RMI Country Coordinator as relevant.

The Advisor will submit monthly timesheets and short monthly activity notes to the PIFS PMU, with confirmation from MAMI of the main activities undertaken. The monthly activity note should summarize days worked, in-country and remote inputs, meetings held, outputs prepared, issues requiring decision, and planned activities for the following month. Technical outputs will be shared with MAMI and PIFS, and PIFS will share them with the World Bank for review or no-objection where required under the project arrangements.

The Advisor will maintain a short action tracker covering agreed activities, responsible counterparts, due dates, risks, dependencies and decisions required. The tracker will be updated at least monthly, and more frequently if requested by the PMU or MAMI. The Advisor will also provide quarterly progress notes against the 12-month payments work plan and a final completion and handover note at the end of the assignment.

Institutional Arrangements

This is a time-based individual consultant assignment contracted by PIFS through the PMU under the Pacific Strengthening CBR Project. The assignment will be undertaken for the benefit of MAMI as the primary country counterpart. The procurement approach is competitive selection of an independent individual consultant, subject to the approved procurement plan, applicable PIFS procurement procedures, conflict-of-interest review, and World Bank review or no-objection requirements where applicable.

The Advisor is expected to spend significant time in Majuro during the assignment, estimated at 50-60 percent of total input days, especially during inception, stakeholder consultations, NPS preparation, payment function setup, capacity building and infrastructure planning. Remote work may be used for document preparation, virtual meetings, training, follow-up and coordination with PIFS and the World Bank.

Office space and access to meeting facilities may be provided by MAMI for in-country inputs and by PIFS for inputs in Suva, subject to availability. The Advisor will be responsible for maintaining secure records of documents, correspondence and data received during the assignment and for complying with all confidentiality requirements.

The Advisor's services will be subject to periodic performance review based on the performance indicators below. Performance review will inform continuation, extension, revision or termination of the assignment, subject to contract terms and World Bank requirements.

 

Performance Indicators

The following performance indicators will be used for contract management and performance assessment. They are intended to measure timely input, quality of advisory support, documented outputs, counterpart engagement and knowledge transfer under a time-based contract:

  • Monthly timesheets are submitted on time and accurately distinguish between in country and remote input days.
  • Monthly activity notes are submitted on time and summarize work undertaken, meetings held, issues requiring decision, risks, planned next steps and counterpart engagement.
  • The Advisor maintains and updates an action tracker covering agreed activities, responsible counterparts, deadlines, dependencies and pending decisions.
  • A 12-month implementation roadmap for MAMI’s national payments function is prepared, discussed with MAMI, PIFS and the World Bank, and updated as required during implementation.
  • The Advisor’s own assignment work plan is maintained and aligned with the 12-month MAMI implementation roadmap, MAMI counterpart availability and agreed priorities.
  • Payment-related IMF MCM recommendations are mapped and separated from broader central banking, governance, accounting, audit, reserve management, HR, communications and corporate services matters.
  • MAMI receives documented advice, meeting notes or working materials on the setup of payment operations and payment oversight responsibilities, including staffing, reporting lines, procedures and capacity needs.
  • MAMI is supported in preparing or refining National Payments Strategy materials, consultation inputs and implementation roadmap elements.
  • Payment infrastructure advice is documented through advisory notes, review comments or options papers that support a phased and fit-for-purpose approach to any future IPCS, without requiring the Advisor to develop systems or detailed technical specifications.
  • Payment system oversight and data work is documented through advisory notes, outlines, review comments, reporting needs, draft structures or training materials, with specialist technical or legal work referred to appropriate experts where required.
  • Stakeholder engagement is documented through meeting notes, action trackers, consultation materials or National Payment Council support materials.
  • Capacity building activities are documented through training materials, attendance records, mentoring notes or handover materials.
  • Quarterly progress notes are submitted against the agreed work plan and discussed with MAMI, PIFS and the World Bank.
  • A final completion and handover note is submitted at the end of the assignment, summarizing work undertaken, outputs prepared, remaining actions, open risks and recommended next steps.
  • The Advisor maintains professional, objective and impartial advice, avoids conflicts of interest, records input days accurately, and complies with PIFS and World Bank rules on confidentiality, anti-corruption and fraud prevention.

Confidentiality and Conflict of Interest

The Payments System Advisor shall comply with PIFS and World Bank policies and rules on anti-corruption, prevention of fraudulent practices, conflict of interest and confidentiality. The Advisor shall maintain confidentiality over all sensitive information obtained during the assignment and shall not publish or disclose any findings, data, reports or recommendations without prior written consent from PIFS and MAMI, and World Bank clearance where required.

Any draft reports and other documents produced by the Advisor will be discussed with and cleared by PIFS, MAMI and the World Bank before final issue. A non-disclosure agreement may be signed between PIFS, MAMI and the selected consultant and attached to the contract.

The Advisor must disclose any actual or potential conflict of interest before contract signature and throughout the assignment. The Advisor shall not participate in downstream procurement activities where such participation would create a conflict of interest under the World Bank Procurement Regulations or the Project Operations Manual.

This is a part-time work assignment, in line with the project timeline; A contract (part-time with a total of 144 days in and year and a maximum of 20 days per month) will initially be signed for two years with a performance based extension every two years thereafter, until 2030. Performance evaluation shall be the basis for the extension or termination of the services. The selected CC is expected to work in his/her home country and will be supported by the PMU based in Suva, Fiji.

Agency Description

The Pacific Islands Forum was established to bring together the region to address pressing issues and challenges, and foster collaboration and cooperation in the pursuit of shared goals. PIF’s mandate is to strengthen cooperation and integration in the Pacific region through the pooling of regional governance, resources and the alignment of policies, furthering Forum members shared goals of economic growth, sustainable development, good governance and security. Founded in 1971, it comprises 18 members: Australia, Cook Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Nauru, New Caledonia, New Zealand, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Republic of Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu.  The PIFS is a vital platform for Leaders to convene, engage in discussions and agree on policies that will benefit the people of the region.

Participating Countries

The Pacific Island Countries (PICs) participating in the regional project comprise Fiji, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu

Overall Project Objective

The Project development Objective is to enable continuous access to correspondent banking services in the participating Pacific Island Countries

Project Length

August 2024 to September 30 2030

2. Project Background

The Pacific Island Forum Secretariat (PIFS) is expecting to receive financing from the World Bank (WB) Group’s International Development Association (IDA) for a proposed project to enable continuous access to correspondent banking services in Pacific Island Countries (PICs).  The PICs covered by the proposed regional project (Fiji, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu) include diverse island economies facing similar correspondent banking relationship challenges.

PICs range in size and topography – from small island states such as Samoa, with two principal inhabited volcanic islands, to large archipelagos such as the Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI), with 29 atolls spread over 2 million km2 of ocean. Population sizes vary from 11,300 people in Tuvalu to 930,000 people in Fiji.

The economic landscape of PICs is equally diverse, marked by different growth drivers, poverty rates, and growth trajectories. The average GDP growth across PICs decelerated to 3.5 percent in 2023 after a historically high of 7.9 percent in 2022, in a rebound from the COVID-19 crisis. However, medium-term growth prospects have worsened, with output growth expected to be significantly below the pre-pandemic trend of 4.7 percent between 2014 & 2019. Given low growth and limited employment opportunities in the island economies, labor migration to neighboring countries and the resulting remittances are critical drivers of living standards.

The United States, New Zealand, and Australia account for 94 percent of the Pacific diaspora. Trade and tourism are vital for many PICs, providing revenue and employment opportunities. Remittances, equivalent to more than 40 percent of GDP in some PICs, are a buffer against income shocks and an important source of finance for essential household consumption and human capital investment.

Financial systems in PICs are characterized by low levels of financial access and an uneven development of national payment systems. Both domestically owned and multinational commercial banks dominate the financial sector in all PICs.  In several PICs, much of the population lacks access to basic transaction accounts, limiting households and businesses’ ability to send and receive payments, save, invest, and respond to climatic and economic shocks. The financial market infrastructure is underdeveloped, in part due to limited competition and the lack of economies of scale. The level of national payment system development is uneven across PICs, and regional efforts to improve the efficiency of cross-border payments are limited in scale and scope.

PICs are uniquely vulnerable to the withdrawal of the correspondent banking relationships (CBR) that underpin international trade, tourism, remittances, and humanitarian financial flows. Correspondent banking is an arrangement under which one bank (correspondent) holds deposits owned by other banks (respondents) and provides payment and other services to those respondent banks. CBRs are an essential feature of the global payment system – they enable individuals, businesses, and governments to make and receive cross-border payment services related to remittances, e-commerce, trade, and official sector flows. The cross-border transactions enabled in PICs are in various currencies, primarily the US dollar, Euro, and Australian dollar.

The withdrawal of CBRs, a well-documented global phenomenon affecting many emerging markets and developing economies, has adverse consequences and negative externalities for Pacific Islanders, including seasonal laborers, small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and vulnerable populations. Based on publicly available data, the number of active correspondents for Pacific banks has declined significantly since 2011 to levels that put the Pacific financial system overall at risk.

In order to mitigate the issues identified above, the WB will provide funding to the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat (PIFS) to implement the proposed “Pacific Strengthening Correspondent Banking Relationships Project”.  The Pacific Islands Forum was established to bring together the region to address pressing issues and challenges and foster collaboration and cooperation in pursuing shared goals. PIF’s mandate is to strengthen cooperation and integration in the Pacific region through the pooling of regional governance, resources, and the alignment of policies, furthering Forum members' shared goals of economic growth, sustainable development, good governance, and security. Founded in 1971, it comprises 18 members: Australia, Cook Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Nauru, New Caledonia, New Zealand, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Republic of Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu.    The PIFS is a vital platform for Leaders to convene, engage in discussions, and agree on policies that will benefit the people of the region.

The project will have two components: (1) Temporary correspondent banking services and (2) Enabling environment and regulatory harmonization.  The proposed project will be implemented by a Project Management Unit (PMU) within the PIFS with strategic project oversight provided by a Project Steering Committee (PSC) comprised of representatives of participating Pacific Finance Ministers. While the PMU will be responsible for day-to-day project activities, it will need to ensure close collaboration and coordination with participating Ministries of Finance, which will oversee project activities and approve work plans through the PSC.

Comprising of Secretaries of Finance or other officials from the participating PICs finance ministries and the PIFS Director (Programs and Initiative), the PSC will meet on a quarterly basis and be responsible for the approval of key project activities as needed. The PSC will report to Pacific Finance Ministers annually at the Forum Economic Minister Meeting (FEMM) to ensure that strategic guidance and orientation are provided over the project activities. At the technical level, each participating PIC will be required to nominate a competent   government official as a Country Focal Point (CFP) responsible for project coordination at the national level, who will be designated as the point of contact with the PMU and the WB team.

The competent government official in each PIC will be complemented by a country coordinator (CC) based in-country, recruited through the PMU, and responsible for coordinating service delivery at the individual country level.

The PIFS is now seeking qualified and competent national consultants from each member country to be the country coordinator (CC) for the PMU and based in the respective participating Pacific Island countries (PICs).  The required positions are expected to be selected by the PIFS in accordance with the WB’s ‘Procurement Regulations for Investment Project Financing (IPF) Borrowers’ (Procurement Regulations), Seventh edition, September 2025, and as amended over time.

3. Objective of the Position

The main objective of the CC would be to manage and coordinate the full range of project, country specific activities during the project cycle from effectiveness through implementation to completion.  The CC will be funded by the project (through the PMU) and report to the PIFS/ PMU Coordinator.  In addition, he/she will work closely with the specific Country Focal Point (CFP), a government official appointed by the MOF of that particular PIC.

 

 

4. Scope of Services

The CC will be required to adopt a flexible approach to coordinate and facilitate the required country specific project activities and report on tangible outcomes in terms of project implementation progress. The CC will be required to work in a pro-active manner, and to help ensure effective implementation of activities and delivery of outputs in a timely manner.

  1. The selected CC will lead and coordinate the day-to-day implementation of the project activities, including the following:
  2. Liaising with PICs Ministry of Finance’s CFP and Central Bank on country specific project related activities, including follow up on the Project Steering Committee (PSC) meetings and preparing meeting minutes as required;
  3. Work in close coordination with the CFP in developing the annual country specific activities, budgets to be submitted to the PIFS/PMU;
  4. Follow up closely on all country specific procurement activities to ensure that there are no delays in the selection process;
  5. In coordination with the CFP, identifying problems/impediments promptly as they arise during project implementation and take timely remedial actions;
  6. Monitoring, with assistance of the PMU M&E specialist, the progress of the country specific project activities and its results indicators;
  7. Follow up closely on all country specific financial management activities to ensure that there are no delays in the payment process;
  8. Follow up closely on the country specific activities and report to the CFP and the PMU Project Coordinator;
  9. Work closely with the CFP and review reports/outputs prepared by selected consultants and provide inputs to the CFP as required;
  10. Prepare the required documentation for the payment of outputs prepared by the selected consultants, obtain CFP approval and submit documents to the PMU for payment;
  11. Work closely with the CFP in preparing annual reports on country specific activities to be submitted to the MOF and PIFS; and
  12. Any other activities as requested by the CFP or the PMU Project Coordinator.

 

5. Reporting Obligations

The CC will work closely with the Country Focal Person (CFP) and report to the PMU Project Coordinator.

 

6. Institutional Arrangements

This is a part-time work assignment, with the Consultant expected to be based in their home country. The Consultant will be supported by the PIFS PMU based in Suva, Fiji but will work closely with and report to the country focal person in the first instance. The CC is expected to show flexibility in working arrangements as time inputs will fluctuate based on country requirements. The work will be part-time, averaging approximately 12  days per month (with a total of 144 days in a year and a maximum of 20 days per month) for the next six years. A contract will initially be signed for two years with a performance based extension every two years thereafter. Performance evaluation shall be the basis for the extension or termination of the services. Facilities such as office space, intercom telephone facilities, personal computers, printing facilities, Internet access and stationery will be provided.

 

7. Performance Indicators

The following performance indicators shall be used for performance assessment:

  1. Positive progress and good performance of the entrusted project activities, as per the TOR;
  2. Ensuring that WB processes and procedures are complied with in all activities and in accordance with the POM;
  3. Provide and maintain strategic engagement, networking and collaboration with key stakeholders;
  4. Ensure the utilization and management of project funds are in compliance with the Financing Agreement;
  5. Ensure the collection of all data required to track project progress;
  6. Ensure the project monitoring and reporting timeline is adhered to;
  7. Prepare and compile periodic semi-annual and annual reports on project activities
  8. Compile proposed annual workplan for the following year with budget and procurement plan;
  9. Positive evaluation of performance by the PIFS and the WB team;
  10. Effective management of other experts engaged by the PMU; and
  11. Support in implementing any capacity building agendas related to the Project as required.

 

8. Confidentiality and Conflict of Interest

The CC undertakes to comply with PIF’s and WB’s policies and rules with regard to anti-corruption and prevention of fraudulent practices, conflict of interest and confidentiality. The CC shall maintain confidentiality on all sensitive information obtained during the assignment and shall not publish wholly or in part the findings or such information, without prior written consent by the PIF. Any draft reports and other documents produced by the consultant will be discussed and cleared with the PIF and the WB before their final issue.
